result.summary: Prometheus makes men and steals fire, and is punished. His son Deucalion survives a great flood and repopulates the earth from stones. The chapter then traces Hellen's line (Dorians, Aeolians, Ionians, Achaeans) and the Aeolid and Aetolian genealogies, with tales of Ceyx and Alcyone, the Aloads, Endymion and Marpessa.

scenes.title: Prometheus steals fire
scenes.summary: Prometheus makes men, gives them fire, and is chained to Caucasus where an eagle eats his liver until Hercules frees him.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus risks and suffers long torment for defying Zeus.

scenes.title: Deucalion and the flood
scenes.summary: Deucalion and Pyrrha survive Zeus's flood in a chest, land on Parnassus, and make new people from stones. They have children including Hellen.
scenes.stakes: Deucalion and Pyrrha face drowning in the flood that destroys mankind.

scenes.title: Hellen and the Aeolid line
scenes.summary: Hellen's sons give their names to Greek peoples, and Aeolus fathers many children.

scenes.title: Ceyx, Alcyone and the Aloads
scenes.summary: Ceyx and Alcyone are turned into birds for their pride. Poseidon's giant sons the Aloads attack the gods and are killed by Artemis's trick.
scenes.stakes: The Aloads risk divine wrath by assaulting heaven; Ceyx and Alcyone are punished for pride.

scenes.title: Endymion and Aetolus
scenes.summary: Endymion founds Elis and sleeps forever; his son Aetolus flees after killing Apis and names Aetolia.

scenes.title: Aetolian genealogy
scenes.summary: Descendants of Aetolus found cities and branch into new families.

scenes.title: Marpessa and Thestius's house
scenes.summary: Idas carries off Marpessa, Evenus drowns himself, and Marpessa chooses Idas over Apollo. Thestius's and Porthaon's children are listed.
scenes.stakes: Marpessa risks being abandoned by a god; Evenus loses his daughter.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic-style name for the brothers Otus and Ephialtes, sons of Aloeus (or Poseidon).

notable_quotes.reason: The famous image of Prometheus's endless punishment by the eagle.
Stones become people, the myth explaining the word laos.

analysis.text: Human origins and divine punishment: Prometheus defies Zeus for mankind's sake, and Zeus later destroys and renews humanity through the flood.
The genealogies explain Greek tribal names and link cities to mythic founders, expressing Greek ethnic identity.

legacy.text: The Prometheus myth became a lasting symbol of defiance and progress, notably in Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound and Shelley's Prometheus Unbound.
Deucalion's flood resembles other Near Eastern flood stories, and 'halcyon days' derives from the kingfisher Alcyone.

fun_facts.text: The Library (Bibliotheca) is attributed to Apollodorus, but the real author is unknown; it likely dates to the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: Fennel stalk: the giant fennel has a hollow stalk with a dry pith that smoulders slowly, so it could carry fire.
Lobes: the rounded divisions of the liver; the nightly regrowth makes the punishment endless.
Chest: the Greek word means a box or ark; it serves as Deucalion's boat in the flood.
The Isthmus is the Isthmus of Corinth, joining central Greece to the Peloponnese; the flood covered everything beyond the region of these mountains.
Zeus, the god of Escape: a cult title of Zeus as saviour, here thanked for delivering Deucalion from the flood.
The pun links Greek laos, 'people', with laas, 'stone'. It is an invented etymology, not a real linguistic derivation.
"Lucifer" here translates Greek Eosphoros, the morning star (Venus as Light-bringer); it is not the Christian devil.
Alcyon is the Greek word for kingfisher; the name Alcyone is linked to it. The Greek ceyx is a sea bird, rendered here as gannet.
"Draw up the waves... pour them into her lap" is a magical act of longing, inviting the sea-god to impregnate her.
A cubit is about the length of a forearm (roughly 18 inches); a fathom is six feet, so the growth is enormous.
"Quarry" means the hunted animal; "darts" are javelins.
Aeolians: one of the main branches of the Greeks, traditionally associated with Thessaly and named after Aeolus, ancestor of this line.
"Some say" marks a variant tradition; the author often notes rival versions of a genealogy without choosing between them.
Naiad: a nymph associated with fresh water, such as springs, rivers and lakes.
"Killed his hosts" is a grave offence in Greek thought, since it violates the sacred duty owed to a host.
"Wooed by Apollo" sets up the later contest; Idas takes her by force in a gift chariot from Poseidon.
"Would have robbed him of the damsel" means Apollo was about to take her away, but was stopped.
The Sirens are the bird-women whose song lures sailors to death, famous from the Odyssey.

context_notes.text: Hephaestus is the smith god, so he is the natural one to fasten Prometheus with chains and nails.
Pandora was made by the gods as the first woman, sent as a punishment to humankind; Pyrrha is her daughter.
Hellen is the legendary ancestor of the Hellenes, the Greeks, who are named after him.
Hellen is the mythical ancestor of all Greeks, who call themselves Hellenes; the name explains the people's identity.
Ossa, Pelion and Olympus are mountains in northern Greece; Olympus was the gods' home, so stacking them aims at heaven.
Naxos is an Aegean island; Artemis is the virgin huntress goddess, so a deer disguise suits her.
The Moon (Selene) loved Endymion; his endless sleep is the best-known part of his myth.
The story explains why the river Lycormas was later called Evenus, a common kind of myth about place names.
Zeus, king of the gods, acts as arbiter when two powerful figures quarrel over a mortal.
Leda, daughter of Thestius, is later known as the mother of Helen and the Dioscuri, though that is not told here.

literary_notes.text: The liver that regrows each night makes the punishment unending, an image of endless suffering for defying the gods.
Humans made from earth and stone echo the earlier creation of men from earth and water, linking the two origin stories.
The couple's pride in likening themselves to Hera and Zeus brings divine punishment, a classic Greek pattern.
The giants' yearly growth and mountain-stacking exaggerate their size and ambition to mythic scale.
The giants' own aim at the deer kills them, so their eagerness destroys them.
Endymion's chosen gift of endless sleep is a strange reward: he gains deathlessness but gives up waking life.
Aetolus's violence toward those who gave him shelter, after fleeing for murder, hints at the bloodshed that runs through this line.
Evenus's despair at failing to catch Idas, killing his horses and drowning himself, makes a short genealogy suddenly tragic.
Marpessa's choice shows her prudence: she fears an immortal's lasting love may fade as she ages, and prefers an equal.
